title: Hard to find
hookLine: a free Saturday slides by on the couch; Shantideva says a day like it is hard to find
carry: a precious human life: rarer than the turtle's yoke
tomorrow: a good thought shows up. why is it gone so fast?

lines: A SATURDAY WITH NOTHING ON IT.
THE DAY SLIDES OFF THE TABLE.
cards: A Saturday with nothing on it. No shift, no practice, no family thing.

It shows up maybe once a season, and here's how it usually goes: you wake late, you pick up the phone to check one thing, and the next time you look up the light has moved across the floor. Nothing went wrong.
Nobody got hurt. The day just slid off the table. Shantideva noticed that same slide, about a whole life instead of a day, and he answered it with a picture from an older sermon.

teach.h: ONE OCEAN, ONE YOKE, ONE BLIND TURTLE.
teach.b: Here's the picture, from the Pali suttas. The Buddha asks his monks to see the whole earth as one ocean. Somewhere on it floats a wooden yoke with a single hole, pushed east by one wind, west by another.
Down in the deep lives a blind turtle that comes up once every hundred years. Would it ever put its neck through that hole?
Only by chance, the monks say. So too, the Buddha says, it is by chance that one gets a human life. Shantideva takes that and turns it toward today.
In the first chapter of his poem, he says this human life, with its leisure and its opportunity, is very hard to find, and it can do what a life is for.
If no good comes of it now, he asks, when will a chance like this come round again? Leisure here doesn't mean a day off.
It means the freedoms you might skip past: a mind clear enough to think, a little time that isn't pure survival, a teaching within reach. The verse isn't trying to scare anyone.

teach.h: NOT A THREAT: LOOK AT THIS.
teach.b: It's closer to a friend grabbing your arm at a window: look at this.
Hard to find, and you're standing in it.

how: Some Tibetan teachers open a course on the Bodhicaryavatara with this verse on the precious human life, and the blind turtle from the Pali suttas is told in more than one Buddhist school as a reminder of how rare the chance is.

o: a hidden temple that only monks know how to reach
a teaching too difficult for most people to grasp
this life with room to learn, rare and easy to waste

games.q: the turtle story — tap the pairs.
p: the whole earth, seen as water
pushed east and west by the winds
comes up once every hundred years
asks when a chance like this comes again

s: the precious human life teaching is meant to make you feel guilty
the verse reads more like a friend at a window: look at this. it points at a chance, not a failure.
the blind turtle comes from the Pali suttas, older than Shantideva's poem
the Buddha tells it to his monks in the Samyutta; Shantideva's verse turns the same idea toward today.
leisure in the verse means a vacation or a day off
it means the room in a life to think and meet a teaching: time that isn't pure survival.

games.q: a friend says, "life's short, so i just try to enjoy it." how does Shantideva's verse use that same fact?
o: the same way: a rare life is for enjoying while it lasts.
a life with leisure is a rare chance to do what a life is for, so use it for good now.
the opposite: life is long, so there's no hurry to practice.
games.why: Shantideva agrees the chance is rare. that's exactly why he asks: if no good comes of it now, when will a chance like this come round again?

practice: Name one freedom you have right now, out loud, in plain words: I can read. I have this hour. Someone taught me this.
Say it once, slowly, then sit with it for the rest of the time, the way you'd look at something you almost walked past.

wordCard.voice: Hard to find. Shantideva's name for this life with room in it: leisure, opportunity, a teaching nearby. Rare as a blind turtle finding the yoke.

orig.note: Sanskrit: hard to get, rare. Shantideva's verse calls this human life very hard to find.

carryVoice: Your line: a precious human life, rarer than the turtle's yoke. The turtle found the hole once; you're already through it. Two days into the poem.

sources.ref: Bodhicaryavatara 1.4 (this human life with leisure and opportunity is very hard to find)
Samyutta Nikaya 56.48 (Chiggala Sutta: the blind turtle and the yoke)
